title: Epicurus, whose name now means fine dining, defined pleasure as the absence of pain

cover.alt: A marble bust of Epicurus, bearded with a furrowed brow, a Roman copy displayed in the Altes Museum, Berlin.

body: Epicurus (341–270 BC) founded a school in Athens around 306 BC that met in his garden, and it welcomed women students, among them Leontion and Themista. His goal was not feasting but ataraxia, freedom from disturbance, and aponia, freedom from bodily pain: pleasure, for him, simply meant the absence of suffering. He also argued that death is nothing to us, since what is dissolved has no sensation. In the Middle Ages he was remembered, inaccurately, as a patron of drunkards and gluttons, and ‘epicure’ came to mean a person of refined taste in food, almost the reverse of his teaching.

right.label: Epicurus
right.text: Pleasure is the absence of pain. Aim for a calm mind (ataraxia) and a body free of pain (aponia).

slides.heading: An open garden
slides.text: The school took its name from the garden Epicurus owned, where it met. It welcomed women during his lifetime, among them Themista, Batis, Leontion and Nikidion. The physics behind the ethics was atomism: everything is atoms moving in empty space, with an occasional random swerve that he used to make room for free will.

slides.heading: Which is not an Epicurean idea?
items: Pleasure is the absence of pain
Life is a feast to be enjoyed
slides.explanation: The first three are Epicurus’s own doctrines. The feast is the later caricature: in the Middle Ages he was wrongly remembered as a patron of drunkards and gluttons.
